title: The Computer at West Street: Betty Shannon, the Wiring of Theseus, and Entropy House
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: New York and New Brunswick: the Scholarship

stops.name: Manhattan, the birth on the fourteenth of April
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in Wikipedia; the borough and the hospital are unrecorded, and the pin is the general Manhattan coordinate rather than a building
stops.campa: Mary Elizabeth Moore is born in New York City to Vilma Ujlaky Moore and James E. Moore. The family calls her Betty, and Betty is the name that will follow her through a mathematics degree, a war desk of hand calculation, a marriage of fifty-two years, and a century that spends seventy of those years crediting her husband for work two people did at one table. The city she is born into already holds the laboratory that will hire her: Bell Telephone Laboratories, a brick block on West Street at the Hudson edge of the Village.
suggested_refs: New York City birth registers for April 1922, which no source consulted has cited for this birth
sources: Wikipedia, 'Betty Shannon'

stops.name: New Brunswick, the full scholarship
stops.date_confidence: the scholarship and the college are attested; no source gives a year of matriculation, and 1940 is a placeholder worked back from her age
stops.campa: The New Jersey College for Women, later Douglass College of Rutgers, takes her on a full scholarship. She reads mathematics. In 1940 a woman studying mathematics in New Brunswick is studying it for its own sake, since the professions that will want her do not yet know they will want her; within four years the calculation of microwave propagation and radar returns will be done by hand, in rooms full of women with pencils, and the country will need every one of them it can find.
suggested_refs: The Douglass College registrar's records at Rutgers, never consulted in any published account of her
sources: Wikipedia, 'Betty Shannon'
Scientific American, Soni and Goodman, 'Betty Shannon, Unsung Mathematical Genius' (24 July 2017)

stops.name: New Brunswick, Phi Beta Kappa in mathematics
stops.date_confidence: the Phi Beta Kappa degree in mathematics is attested; no source consulted gives the graduation year, and 1944 is inferred from the Bell Labs hiring that follows
stops.campa: She graduates Phi Beta Kappa with a degree in mathematics. The key and the discipline are the two facts the record keeps; her marks, her teachers, her thesis if she wrote one, and the year itself are absent from every source that mentions her. What survives of this campus in the literature is one clause in one sentence, repeated by every later writer from a single origin, because everything written about Betty Moore is written later and for another reason: she married Claude Shannon.
suggested_refs: The Phi Beta Kappa chapter rolls of the New Jersey College for Women
sources: Wikipedia, 'Betty Shannon'
Scientific American, Soni and Goodman (24 July 2017)

stops.name: 463 West Street, hired as a computer
stops.date_confidence: the hiring is attested, its date is not; the year follows the inferred graduation, and the pin is the atlas's canonical West Street coordinate rather than a geocoder's 40.7367,-74.0096
stops.campa: Bell Telephone Laboratories hires her into the mathematics department as a computer. The word is a job title, not a machine: one of the women who perform the calculations the engineers need and do not have time to grind out, arithmetic done by hand and by desk calculator, checked twice, handed up. The building is 463 West Street, headquarters and laboratory both, and it will stay headquarters until 1967. Everything she does for the next several years is done inside it or dispatched from it.
suggested_refs: The Bell Telephone Laboratories building at 463 West Street, now the Westbeth artists' housing
sources: Scientific American, Soni and Goodman (24 July 2017)
Wikipedia, 'Bell Labs' (for the 1967 relocation to Murray Hill)

stops.name: 463 West Street, the microwaves
stops.date_confidence: the microwave work is attested without dates; 1945 is a placeholder inside the war years
stops.campa: She works as a numerical analyst on the mathematics of microwaves. The war runs on this arithmetic and the arithmetic runs on women; the men whose names go on the reports depend on rooms of them, and the rooms are not named. Two years before she arrives, Alan Turing spent two months in this building on secure speech and took tea with a young mathematician named Claude Shannon in the cafeteria downstairs. She is not in that room and no source puts her there. She will meet him in this building anyway, five years late.
suggested_refs: Bell Labs wartime microwave research reports, which carry the engineers' names and not the computers'
sources: Wikipedia, 'Betty Shannon'
Scientific American, Soni and Goodman (24 July 2017)

stops.name: Whippany, the radar group
stops.date_confidence: the transfer to the radar group is attested; no source dates it, and the Whippany coordinate is the Bell Labs radar site rather than an address given in any document about her
stops.campa: She transfers out of microwave work into the radar research group. Radar is the Laboratories' other war, run from the New Jersey site at Whippany, and the calculation it demands is the same calculation done faster and against a deadline that moves. She is good at it, and the reports carry other names. The record of what she computed there survives nowhere; what survives is the job description, four words long, in an encyclopedia article written seventy years later about somebody's wife.

segments.name: The Courtship: Two Apartments and One Laboratory

stops.name: 463 West Street, meeting Claude Shannon
stops.date_confidence: the fall of 1948 is attested by Scientific American; month and day are defaulted, and the site follows the Manhattan headquarters rather than Murray Hill, which the Laboratories do not make headquarters until 1967
stops.campa: In the fall she meets Claude Shannon. He is thirty-two, recently the author of a paper that has cut the theory of communication loose from its wires, and famously impatient with anyone he does not take for his equal; he would not, she says later, go out of his way to collaborate with other people. She is twenty-six and has been doing his colleagues' arithmetic for four years. He asks her out, and Wikipedia records that they then dine together nightly.
stops.quote: wouldn't go out of his way to collaborate with other people
stops.quote_source: Betty Shannon on Claude Shannon, quoted in Jimmy Soni and Rob Goodman, "Betty Shannon, Unsung Mathematical Genius," Scientific American, 24 July 2017
suggested_refs: The Bell Labs mathematics department at 463 West Street in 1948
sources: Scientific American, Soni and Goodman (24 July 2017)
Wikipedia, 'Betty Shannon'

stops.name: East Eighteenth Street, her own apartment
stops.date_confidence: 1948 attested; month and day defaulted, and the coordinate is East Eighteenth Street between Union Square and Irving Place, the block the source names without giving a number
stops.campa: She keeps rooms on East Eighteenth Street and he keeps rooms in the West Village, and for the length of the courtship the two of them commute between the two addresses and the one laboratory. The geography is small and entirely Manhattan. It is also the argument against the story that puts them in New Jersey: two people who split their evenings between Union Square and Greenwich Village are not driving out to Murray Hill for the workday that ends those evenings.
suggested_refs: East Eighteenth Street between Union Square and Irving Place, Manhattan
sources: Scientific American, Soni and Goodman (24 July 2017)

stops.name: Greenwich Village, the books printed in two parts
stops.date_confidence: 1948 attested for the courtship; the month is a placeholder and the pin is Claude Shannon's Village rooms, since the source names no address for the playing
stops.campa: What she remembers of falling in love is not mathematics. She plays piano; he plays clarinet. They come home from the Laboratories and find books of music printed in two parts, and they play the two parts. She gives that account in her own voice seventy years on, when somebody finally asks her. Later writers build a case for an intellectual partnership out of the marriage, and the only description of its beginning that survives in her words is two people playing duets after work in a rented room.
stops.quote: I played piano and he played clarinet, and we'd come home from work, and we found some books of music that had two parts, and we'd enjoy playing together.
stops.quote_source: Betty Shannon, quoted in Jimmy Soni and Rob Goodman, "Betty Shannon, Unsung Mathematical Genius," Scientific American, 24 July 2017
suggested_refs: Claude Shannon's West Village rooms during the 1948 courtship
sources: Scientific American, Soni and Goodman (24 July 2017)

stops.name: Murray Hill, the marriage
stops.date_confidence: the date is contradicted in print: MacTutor gives 27 March 1949 and Scientific American gives 22 March 1949, and neither shows its working. The 27th is carried to match the atlas's existing Shannon pin. The venue is unrecorded in every source consulted, and the marker follows her workplace rather than a document
stops.campa: Mary Elizabeth Moore marries Claude Shannon in March of 1949, five months after the first dinner. She describes the proposal as not very formal. No source names the church, the registry office, the city, or the witnesses; two published biographies name two different days of the same month and neither explains itself. The atlas plants the marker on the laboratory, because a laboratory is the only place both of them are documented to have been that spring, and calls the pin what it is.
stops.quote_source: Betty Shannon on Claude Shannon's proposal, quoted in Jimmy Soni and Rob Goodman, "Betty Shannon, Unsung Mathematical Genius," Scientific American, 24 July 2017

segments.name: Murray Hill: the Memorandum and the Mouse

stops.name: Murray Hill, Composing Music by a Stochastic Process
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the memorandum's own date; the memorandum itself was not read in this pass and is known only through citation
stops.campa: Eight months married, she signs a Bell Telephone Laboratories technical memorandum with John R. Pierce: Composing Music by a Stochastic Process, number MM-49-150-29. Mary E. Shannon, on the cover of a research report, in 1949. The subject is music generated by chance according to fixed probabilities, which is to say her husband's theory turned toward the two-part books. Two information theorists writing sixty-eight years later call the credit exceptional, and they mean the word literally: it is the exception.
stops.quote: significant and unusual achievement for a woman to get her name on a research report
stops.quote_source: Haizi Yu and Lav R. Varshney, IEEE Information Theory Society Newsletter, December 2017, as quoted in Wikipedia, 'Betty Shannon'
suggested_refs: Bell Telephone Laboratories Technical Memorandum MM-49-150-29, 15 November 1949, cited everywhere and read by nobody in this pass
sources: Pierce and Shannon, BTL Technical Memorandum MM-49-150-29 (cited in Wikipedia, 'Betty Shannon')
Yu and Varshney, IEEE Information Theory Society Newsletter (December 2017)

stops.name: Greenwich Village, the unicycle at Christmas
stops.date_confidence: Christmas is attested and the year is taken from Waldrop's account of the first year of the marriage; the house is unnamed in every source, so the pin follows the couple's last documented address
stops.campa: For Christmas she gives her husband a unicycle. He rides it around the house, and then along the corridors of the Laboratories, and the image outlasts most of his theorems in the public memory: the father of information theory on one wheel, juggling, passing colleagues who have stopped pretending to be surprised. The gift is hers. In every retelling of that corridor it is his eccentricity being described, and the fact that somebody went out and bought him the wheel drops quietly out of the story.
stops.quote: He had been a gymnast in college, so he was better at it than you might have thought.
stops.quote_source: Betty Shannon, quoted in M. Mitchell Waldrop, "Claude Shannon: Reluctant Father of the Digital Age," MIT Technology Review, 2001
suggested_refs: The unicycle photographs from the Bell Labs corridors, reproduced in every Shannon profile
sources: MIT Technology Review, Waldrop (2001)

stops.name: Murray Hill, the wiring of Theseus
stops.date_confidence: 1950 attested for Theseus; the month is unrecorded and defaulted, and the site follows the atlas's existing Shannon pin
stops.campa: Theseus is a mechanical mouse that learns a maze: relays under the floor remember, and on the second run the mouse goes straight to the cheese. It is one of the first machines anybody builds that visibly learns, and it is demonstrated for decades as his. Scientific American, written by the biographers who had the family's papers, states it flatly: it was Betty, not Claude, who completed the wiring for Theseus the mouse. His own 1952 paper on the mouse does not mention her.
suggested_refs: Theseus and its maze, held by the MIT Museum
sources: Scientific American, Soni and Goodman (24 July 2017)
Wikipedia, 'Betty Shannon'
Wikipedia, 'Claude Shannon'

stops.name: Murray Hill, the handwriting in the papers
stops.date_confidence: undated: Betty Shannon describes the practice across early and later papers without fixing a year, and 1950 is a placeholder inside the Murray Hill decade
stops.campa: She edits what he writes, fills the gaps he leaves in the mathematics because they are obvious to him, and adds the historical references he cannot be troubled with. She also copies. Decades later, people sorting the Shannon manuscripts hit pages in a hand that is not his and cannot account for them. The confusion is the evidence: a collaborator invisible enough that her handwriting reads as an anomaly in the file rather than as the second person in the room.
stops.quote: Some of his early papers and even later papers are in my handwriting...and not in his, which confused people at first.
stops.quote_source: Betty Shannon, quoted in Jimmy Soni and Rob Goodman, "Betty Shannon, Unsung Mathematical Genius," Scientific American, 24 July 2017
suggested_refs: The Claude Elwood Shannon papers at the Library of Congress, where the second hand appears
sources: Scientific American, Soni and Goodman (24 July 2017)

stops.name: Murray Hill, the guessing game in the parlor
stops.date_confidence: the experiments are attested to the early 1950s without a date; 1951 is set against the published entropy of printed English, and the pin replaces an earlier fabricated midpoint in Union Township with the atlas's Murray Hill coordinate
stops.campa: Four people in a living room: Betty, Claude, Bernard Oliver, and Oliver's wife. One supplies the opening letters of a word or a sentence, the others guess how it continues, and the count of right guesses measures how much of written English is redundant. The paper that comes out of this is called Prediction and Entropy of Printed English and it carries one name. The quantity being measured takes its name, by an undated and much disputed anecdote, from John von Neumann telling Shannon that nobody knows what entropy is.
suggested_refs: Claude Shannon, 'Prediction and Entropy of Printed English' (1951), whose experimental subjects go unnamed
sources: IEEE Spectrum, 'Claude Shannon: Tinkerer, Prankster, and Father of Information Theory'

stops.name: Washington, the trip she is not on
stops.date_confidence: May 1951 is attested for Claude Shannon's service on the Special Cryptologic Advisory Group; nothing places Betty Shannon in Washington, and this stop exists to record the absence rather than a presence
stops.campa: Her husband sits on the Special Cryptologic Advisory Group in Washington. The atlas keeps the cipher wing close together: al-Kindi, Trithemius, Whitfield Diffie, Martin Hellman, and the 1949 secrecy paper that will pass between them. Betty Shannon is queued into that wing by marriage and by nothing else. No source consulted describes her working on ciphers, in Washington or anywhere; her own account of the courtship is about duets. The pin is here to hold the gap open rather than to close it.

stops.name: Murray Hill, the birth of Robert James
stops.date_confidence: no source gives a birth date; Wikipedia states that Robert James Shannon died in 1998 aged 45, which puts the birth in 1952 or 1953, before the 1956 move to Massachusetts. The month is arbitrary and the pin follows the parents' documented workplace
stops.campa: The first child is born, a son, Robert James Shannon. No source records the day, the month, or the year; the year is recoverable only by subtracting forty-five from the year of his death. Two more will follow, Andrew Moore and Margarita, called Peggy, and their birth dates are not recorded either. MacTutor lists four children and gets there by splitting Robert James into two boys, which is one more contradiction the record hands over without settling.

stops.name: MIT, the return to Cambridge
stops.date_confidence: 1956 attested for the visiting appointment; month unrecorded and defaulted
stops.campa: Claude Shannon joins the MIT faculty as a visiting professor and the household turns north. He has been at the Laboratories nearly twenty years and she has been in them longer than the marriage has lasted. Cambridge is where he was the graduate student with the differential analyzer; it will also be, thirteen years from now, the place where a young cryptographer named Martin Hellman is handed the 1949 secrecy paper by Peter Elias and reads it as an instruction. The Shannons arrive as a family of five.

stops.name: Winchester, the house on Mystic Lake
stops.date_confidence: 1956 attested for the move; month unrecorded and defaulted, and the pin is the atlas's canonical Winchester coordinate rather than the 42.4523,-71.1467 an earlier pass reused six times
stops.campa: They take a stuccoed house on Mystic Lake in Winchester and keep it more than thirty years. Visitors call it Entropy House. Three children are raised in it and a working population of machines accumulates around them: a chess machine that talks, a motorized pogo stick, a device that matches pennies and appears to read minds, a figure of W. C. Fields juggling three balls on a drumhead. It is a household organized as a laboratory, and both of the adults in it are laboratory people.
suggested_refs: Entropy House on Mystic Lake, Winchester, Massachusetts
sources: MIT News, obituary of Claude Shannon (2001)

stops.name: Winchester, the duet books again
stops.date_confidence: undated: the music is attested for the courtship and described as a habit without dates, and 1958 is a placeholder inside the Winchester years
stops.campa: The piano and the clarinet come to Winchester with everything else. She had described the evening duets as the thing that made her fall in love with him; in a house on a lake in Massachusetts the same two-part books get opened after dinner for thirty years. The habit and the instruments are attested. No evening is dated and no piece is named, and the only person who ever described any of it was asked about it once, in her nineties, by two men writing a book about her husband.

stops.name: Las Vegas, the casino test
stops.date_confidence: Edward Thorp's account has the device operational in June 1961 and the Shannons and Thorps meeting in Las Vegas for a casino test in the summer of 1961, both wives taking part; the day is defaulted. An earlier research pass flagged Betty's presence as unconfirmed, and Thorp refutes that flag
stops.campa: Two couples go to Nevada with a machine hidden in a shoe. The device is the first wearable computer, built by Claude Shannon and Edward Thorp in the Winchester basement to predict where a roulette ball will fall; it is operational in June and the test comes in the summer. Both wives are on the trip and both take part. What Betty does at the table is not written down, only that she is at it, which is more than the atlas can say for the Harvey Prize, the Kyoto Prize, or any other room he was photographed in.
suggested_refs: Edward Thorp's account of the Shannon roulette computer and the summer 1961 Las Vegas test
sources: Edward O. Thorp, account of the Shannon-Thorp roulette computer

stops.name: Winchester, the workshop
stops.date_confidence: the gadgets are attested for the Winchester years without dates; 1963 is a placeholder inside them
stops.campa: The building never stops. The house fills with things that move: the talking chess machine, the pogo stick with a motor in it, the Hex machine, the penny matcher. Every one of them is catalogued as his. She had wired Theseus in 1950 and no paper said so, and nothing in the record requires the assumption that the pattern changed when the workshop moved to Massachusetts. There is also no source that says it did not. The atlas records the workshop as a household and leaves the hands unassigned.

stops.name: Winchester, the investment library
stops.date_confidence: undated: the stock market partnership is attested without dates and 1965 is a placeholder inside the Winchester decades
stops.campa: The shelves fill with economics and investment. They research the market together and they buy early into the companies coming out of Santa Clara County, and the family's money is made this way rather than by information theory, which pays a professor's salary. Their daughter, asked about it long afterward, refuses the version in which the mathematician had the ideas and the wife kept the books. It was a joint project. This is the only claim about Betty Shannon's working life that comes from inside the family.
stops.quote: Their work in the stock market was completely a team effort. It is not the case that my father had these mathematical ideas about the stock market and then figured out how to put them to work to make money...It was always a joint project.
stops.quote_source: Margarita (Peggy) Shannon, quoted in Jimmy Soni and Rob Goodman, "Betty Shannon, Unsung Mathematical Genius," Scientific American, 24 July 2017

stops.name: MIT, the secrecy paper goes out the door
stops.date_confidence: 1969 is attested for Peter Elias handing Hellman the paper; the month is unrecorded and defaulted. Whether Betty Shannon's hand touched that particular manuscript is not stated by any source and is not claimed here
stops.campa: At MIT, Peter Elias hands Martin Hellman a copy of Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems, published in 1949. Hellman reads it and finds the proof that perfect secrecy is possible and expensive; out of that reading, and out of Whitfield Diffie arriving at the same door from another direction, comes public key cryptography and the shape of every private message sent since. The paper dates from the first year of the marriage, the period in which, by her own account, his papers came out in her handwriting.
suggested_refs: Claude Shannon, 'Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems' (1949), the copy Peter Elias passed on

stops.name: Boston, the Weavers' Guild
stops.date_confidence: undated: Wikipedia records the membership without a year, and 1970 is a placeholder set before the attested 1976 deanship
stops.campa: She takes up weaving and joins the Weavers' Guild of Boston. No source connects the loom to the mathematics, and this file will not connect them either; the two careers sit side by side in the one paragraph anybody has written about her, unexplained. A loom is a machine that stores a pattern and executes it thread by thread, and the woman at this one spent the war computing by hand and spent 1950 wiring a mouse that learned. The sources say nothing about that. It is recorded here as adjacency.

stops.name: Boston, Dean of the Weavers' Guild
stops.date_confidence: the 1976 to 1978 deanship is attested; months are unrecorded and defaulted
stops.campa: She serves two years as Dean of the Weavers' Guild of Boston. It is the only office she is recorded as holding anywhere, in any institution, in ninety-five years. Bell Telephone Laboratories gave her a job title and one co-authored memorandum; the Guild gives her a title with her own name attached to it and a term of years. The two years run to 1978, the year her husband retires from MIT, and the encyclopedia gives the deanship the same single sentence it gives the radar group.

stops.name: Boston, the Distinguished Achievement Award
stops.date_confidence: attested and undated: Wikipedia gives no year and no other source dates it. 1978 is a placeholder set immediately after the deanship, and an earlier research pass's 'c. 1978' was an invention, disclosed here rather than repeated
stops.campa: The Weavers' Guild of Boston gives her its Distinguished Achievement Award. Nobody wrote down when. It is the only prize of her own in the record, set against her husband's National Medal of Science, his Harvey Prize, his Kyoto Prize, and the award that carries his name and is given at MIT to other people. A guild of weavers kept better track of her than the laboratory did, and even the guild did not keep the date. The atlas places the award here because it has to place it somewhere.

stops.name: MIT, the retirement
stops.date_confidence: 1978 attested for the retirement and 1958 to 1978 for the Donner chair; the month is unrecorded and defaulted
stops.campa: Claude Shannon retires from the MIT faculty, twenty-two years after arriving and twenty years into the Donner chair. He is sixty-two, and he withdraws into the Winchester house where the machines are. The person who has been managing that household, the papers, the money and the collection is fifty-six and has just finished two years running a guild. The public record of the next fifteen years is almost entirely a record of him, written by visitors she let in and fed.

stops.campa: Journalists come to Winchester in the late years and she lets them in, feeds them, and answers for a man who is beginning not to answer. She insists on the building. He still built things, she tells them, and describes a small figure of W. C. Fields bouncing three balls on a drumhead, which is a juggling machine made by a man who juggled and who rode a unicycle his wife bought him. The pieces are printed as portraits of him. She is the one being interviewed.

stops.name: Winchester, the diagnosis
stops.date_confidence: MIT Technology Review dates the family's confirmation to mid-1993; the day is defaulted. An earlier pass left this undated and called her a caregiver-adjacent survivor, which the same source contradicts
stops.campa: By the middle of 1993 the family confirms what visitors have been guessing: Claude Shannon has Alzheimer's disease. He is seventy-seven. The theory that gave the century its unit is intact in every engineering school on earth and gone from the head that made it. She is seventy-one. From here to his death she is the one who explains him to the world and corrects the record when it is wrong about him. When he cannot travel to a ceremony, she accepts the honours in his place.

The atlas can attest the facility, the year, and that she went. It cannot attest a single visit.

stops.campa: Claude Shannon dies at the Courtyard Nursing Care Center at eighty-four. The obituaries run everywhere, and the MIT notice lists the survivors in order: his wife Betty, his son Andrew Moore of Brookline, his daughter Margarita of Cambridge, a sister, two granddaughters. She is fifty-two years married and named first, which is the convention, and she is also the last living person who watched those papers being written. The scale of the response astonishes her, and she says so.

What she does with them is not recorded anywhere reachable: no interviews except the one, no memoir, no papers deposited under her own name, no oral history taken by any of the institutions that owe their field to her household. She is in her eighties, then her nineties, eight miles from the lake house, while the century turns into the thing her husband described.

stops.campa: Mary Elizabeth Moore Shannon dies at Brookhaven at ninety-five. She had been a human computer at Bell Telephone Laboratories, a numerical analyst on microwaves and on radar, co-author of a 1949 technical memorandum on composing music by chance, the hand that wired Theseus, the second reader and frequently the copyist of the papers that founded information theory, an investor, and Dean of the Weavers' Guild of Boston. The obituaries call her the widow of Claude Shannon.

Her husband has a bronze in Gaylord, a bust at the Laboratories, a doodle on the world's search engine for his centenary, and an award given in his name at MIT to other people. stops.campa: Eleven weeks after her death, Jimmy Soni and Rob Goodman publish Betty Shannon, Unsung Mathematical Genius in Scientific American. It appears six days after their biography of her husband and is built from the same research; it is the book's own Betty material, given a headline of its own rather than assembled as an independent reassessment. Almost everything anyone quotes her saying comes from this one piece. Whether she read the book, or knew the article was coming, no source records.
